I am fifty-five, never spent a day in school, and I have farmed these same 8 mu in Quzhou County my whole life. My husband and I manage the land together — our children work in the city now, so it is mostly us two. I do not read books or listen much to the extension agent on the radio. I watch what the successful families in my village do, and I stick with what has filled our bellies in the past.

This year I will plant winter wheat on 7.2 mu, just like always. I will sow around the tenth of October, using about 30 jin of improved wheat seed per mu — half saved from last year and half bought from the seed shop in town. Before sowing I will rotary-till the soil to break up the stubble. For fertilizer, I spread one bag of compound fertilizer per mu as a base, and later I broadcast one bag of ammonium bicarbonate. I know that is a good amount because two years ago I tried to save money and skipped the bicarbonate, and the wheat turned yellow and thin. I will irrigate three times: once before winter so the plants survive the cold, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. I will spray pesticide six times — herbicide once to kill the weeds, insecticide four times when I see aphids, and fungicide once if the leaves spot.

Right after we cut the wheat in early June, we have only a few days to get the summer maize in the ground. There is no time to plough, so we plant directly into the wheat stubble with no-tillage. I use one package of hybrid maize seed per mu — Denghai or Nongda, whatever the shop has in stock. I put down about 80 jin of compound fertilizer per mu at planting. Maize does not need as much water as wheat, but I will irrigate twice if the sky stays dry, especially when it is tasseling. I spray about six times too, mainly for insects and to keep the weeds down.

I keep 0.8 mu for cotton. Cotton is hard work — it needs a lot of spraying and picking — but the price is sometimes better than maize, and it is my backup if grain prices drop. I rotary-till that plot and plant the local improved cotton seed. I use one bag of compound fertilizer for base and another bag for topdressing, and I irrigate three times. Even though the cotton patch is small, I have to spray it many times, maybe eight times through the season, or the bollworms will eat everything.

I do not know exactly how many kilograms of nitrogen or phosphorus that is — I think in bags. But I know my total costs, and I know that skimping on fertilizer is risking hunger, so I would rather spend the money now than regret it later.
